The Story of Medicine-Giving

I bow to Lord Jina, the word of Jina, and the feet of Jain monks, and I write the story related to medicine-giving.

Being free from disease, having constant cheerfulness on the face, attaining wealth and prosperity, becoming beautiful, radiant and strong, and ultimately attaining the happiness of heaven or liberation — these are all fruits of medicine-giving. Therefore, those who wish to be happy should give faultless medicine. Many noble souls have attained fruit through this medicine-giving. Writing about all of them is certainly impossible for me of limited intelligence, let alone for others. Among them, the pure character of Vrushabsena is briefly written here. Wherever the Acharyas have mentioned the giver of medicine, Vrushabsena's name mostly comes. I too follow her example.

In the Janapad region of this India, made sacred by the birth of the Lord, there is a city named Kaveri, filled with all manner of excellent wealth and therefore surpassing heaven's beauty with its own beauty. At the time of this story, the king of Kaveri was Ugrasen. Ugrasen was a true well-wisher of his subjects and a good scholar of statecraft.

In that city lived a good householder merchant named Dhanpati. He had extreme love for the worship and propagation of Lord Jina. His wife Dhanashri was like a second Lakshmi in his house. Dhanashri was chaste and very simple-hearted. Through past merit, they had a daughter named Vrushasena, as beautiful as a celestial princess. Truly, what is not attained through the ripening of merit?

Vrushasena's nurse was beautiful and always bathed her. The water from her bathing collected in a pit. One day, while the beautiful Vrushasena was being bathed, a severely diseased dog fell into the pit where Vrushasena's bath water was collecting. What a wonder — when it came out of that water, it appeared completely healthy! The beautiful nurse was amazed to see this. She thought, 'Ordinary water cannot remove disease like this. But this is Vrushasena's bath water. Some part of her merit must be in it. It seems Vrushasena is a very fortunate girl. It is no wonder that this girl in human form will become a celestial nymph.'

The nurse, inspired by this miracle, began giving that water to sick people. Many were cured. Word of Vrushasena's merit-suffused water spread far and wide. The king himself came to see her and was deeply impressed by her virtue. He honoured her family greatly and gave them many gifts.

Vrushasena grew up to be a devoted Jain. She practised charity, especially medicine-giving, throughout her life. Through the power of her merit, she eventually became a queen and continued her charitable works on a grand scale. She built hospitals, supported physicians, and ensured that medicine was freely available to all. Through her lifelong practice of medicine-giving, she purified her soul and ultimately attained liberation.

This story teaches that medicine-giving is a supremely meritorious act. Even the bath water of a virtuous child had the power to heal a diseased dog. Imagine the merit of consciously giving medicine to the sick! The wise should practise medicine-giving with devotion, for it brings health, beauty, and ultimately liberation.
